experiments.heatEngines.title: Thermodynamic Heat Cycles & Heat Engines
experiments.heatEngines.description: Comprehensive simulation of Carnot, Otto, Diesel, and Stirling heat cycles, featuring live Pressure-Volume (PV) and Temperature-Entropy (TS) indicator diagrams, net work calculations, and real-mode thermal losses.
heatEngines.cycleType_desc: Select thermodynamic cycle under study (Carnot, Otto, Diesel, Stirling)
heatEngines.th_desc: Hot source temperature or peak combustion temperature in Kelvin
heatEngines.tc_desc: Cold sink / ambient intake temperature in Kelvin
heatEngines.compressionRatio_desc: Ratio of maximum to minimum cylinder volume (Vmax / Vmin)
heatEngines.cutOffRatio_desc: Ratio of cylinder volume after fuel injection to clearance volume in Diesel cycle
heatEngines.gasType_desc: Molecular structure and degrees of freedom of working fluid
heatEngines.moles_desc: Number of moles of trapped gas inside cylinder
heatEngines.rpm_desc: Crankshaft rotational speed and cycle frequency
heatEngines.friction_desc: Mechanical drag between piston rings and cylinder wall
heatEngines.heatLeak_desc: Parasitic thermal conduction through cylinder walls to ambient
heatEngines.real_th_effect: In real mode, heat conduction lowers the effective peak temperature
heatEngines.real_friction_effect: Mechanical friction dissipates a fraction of piston net work
heatEngines.real_leak_effect: Cylinder heat leaks reduce net work output and cycle efficiency
heatEngines.formula_carnot: Carnot limit: Maximum possible theoretical efficiency for any heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs
heatEngines.formula_work: First Law: Net output work equals the enclosed loop area on the PV indicator diagram and Qin - Qout
heatEngines.formula_otto: Otto cycle efficiency depends exclusively on the compression ratio r and adiabatic index gamma
heatEngines.formula_diesel: Diesel efficiency depends on both compression ratio r and cut-off ratio rc
heatEngines.formula_power: Mechanical power output equals work per cycle multiplied by cycle frequency
heatEngines.carnot_stroke1: 1→2: Reversible Isothermal Expansion at Th (Qin absorbed)
heatEngines.carnot_stroke2: 2→3: Reversible Isentropic Expansion (Temp drops Th -> Tc)
heatEngines.carnot_stroke3: 3→4: Reversible Isothermal Compression at Tc (Qout rejected)
heatEngines.carnot_stroke4: 4→1: Reversible Isentropic Compression (Temp rises Tc -> Th)
heatEngines.diesel_stroke2: 2→3: Isobaric Heat Addition (Constant pressure fuel injection)
heatEngines.stirling_stroke1: 1→2: Isothermal Expansion at hot reservoir Th
heatEngines.stirling_stroke3: 3→4: Isothermal Compression at cold sink Tc
heatEngines.stirling_stroke4: 4→1: Isochoric Heating (Regenerator delivers heat to gas)
heatEngines.theoryP1: A heat engine is a thermodynamic system that receives thermal energy from a high-temperature reservoir, converts part of it into net mechanical work, and rejects the remaining heat to a lower-temperature sink.
heatEngines.theoryP2: According to the Second Law of Thermodynamics (Kelvin-Planck statement), no engine operating in a cycle can convert all absorbed heat into work without discharging waste heat. The theoretical upper limit of thermal efficiency is given by the reversible Carnot cycle: η_max = 1 - Tc/Th.
heatEngines.theoryP3: Internal combustion engines (Otto and Diesel) and external combustion systems (Stirling) convert gas expansion into rotary motion through pistons and crankshafts. Net work output is given by the closed path integral on the indicator diagram: W_net = ∮ P dV.
